Appendix C • Approximate Velocity Units in Single-Snapshot Calculations [3.2.3]

C.1 From the exact logarithmic coordinate to the Hubble-flow approximation

In Appendix B we showed that, after centering the spectral coordinate on the rest-frame wavelength of a given transition \(j\), the exact logarithmic coordinate may be written as \begin{align} u_{\mathrm{exact}}^{(j)}(x) = c\ln\!\left( \frac{a_\dagger}{a(x)} \right), \tag{C.1} \end{align} where \(x\) denotes the comoving position along the line of sight, and \(a_\dagger\) is a chosen reference scale factor.

To understand how this quantity changes along the skewer, we differentiate with respect to \(x\): \begin{align} \frac{d u_{\mathrm{exact}}^{(j)}}{dx} &= -c\,\frac{1}{a(x)}\frac{da}{dx} = -c\,\frac{d\ln a}{dx}. \tag{C.2} \end{align} Using \begin{align} a=\frac{1}{1+z}, \qquad \frac{d\ln a}{dz}=-\frac{1}{1+z}, \qquad dx=\frac{c}{H(z)}\,dz, \tag{C.3} \end{align} it follows that \begin{align} \frac{d\ln a}{dx} = \frac{d\ln a}{dz}\frac{dz}{dx} = -\frac{1}{1+z}\frac{H(z)}{c}, \tag{C.4} \end{align} and therefore \begin{align} \frac{d u_{\mathrm{exact}}^{(j)}}{dx} = \frac{H(z)}{1+z}. \tag{C.5} \end{align} Integrating from a reference point \(x_\dagger\), chosen such that \(u_{\mathrm{exact}}^{(j)}(x_\dagger)=0\), we obtain \begin{align} u_{\mathrm{exact}}^{(j)}(x) = \int_{x_\dagger}^{x} \frac{H[z(x')]}{1+z(x')}\,dx'. \tag{C.6} \end{align} This makes explicit that the exact logarithmic coordinate may be interpreted as the accumulated Hubble-flow contribution along the line of sight.

If the redshift interval covered by one simulation box is sufficiently narrow, then the factor \(H(z)/(1+z)\) varies only mildly across the box and may be approximated by its value at the snapshot redshift \(z_{\mathrm{box}}\). In that case, \begin{align} u_H(x) \coloneqq u_{\mathrm{exact}}^{(j)}(x) \approx \frac{H(z_{\mathrm{box}})}{1+z_{\mathrm{box}}} \int_{x_\dagger}^{x}dx' = \frac{H(z_{\mathrm{box}})}{1+z_{\mathrm{box}}}(x-x_\dagger). \tag{C.7} \end{align} This is the Hubble-flow part of the practical single-snapshot coordinate.
